title: How a browser extension reaches the page
purpose: Show which part of an extension touches the page and why the manifest permissions decide what it can see.
explanation: The manifest declares the extension parts and the permissions they get. A content script runs in the page and reads or changes the DOM. A DevTools page adds a panel to DevTools. Both send messages to the background script, which holds shared state, and a popup or panel shows the result. Every tool in your toolkit uses this same structure, so its permissions tell you what data it can read.
alt: Flowchart: manifest.json with permissions and host access points to the background script, the content script and the DevTools page. The content script reads and changes the page DOM and sends messages to the background script. The DevTools page also sends messages to the background script, which feeds a popup or panel that shows results.

learning_check.question: An accessibility extension must read the headings on every page you open. Which part of the extension does that, and what in the manifest allows it?
learning_check.answer: A content script reads the page DOM. Host permissions (or matches for the content script) in manifest.json decide on which sites it may run.

title: Parts of a WebExtension and who talks to whom
purpose: Show the parts that manifest.json can declare and which of them touch the page.
explanation: manifest.json is the only required file. It points to the background script, content scripts, popup, sidebar and options pages, and web accessible resources. A content script works on the page DOM and talks to the background script by messages. It talks to page scripts only through window.postMessage. Popups, sidebars and options pages can use the same privileged APIs as the background script.
alt: Flowchart: manifest.json points to a background script, a content script, popup sidebar and options pages, and web accessible resources. The content script reads and changes the page DOM, sends messages to the background script and uses window.postMessage to reach page scripts. Popup, sidebar and options pages use the same APIs as the background script.

learning_check.question: How can a content script ask the browser to run an API it is not allowed to call itself?
learning_check.answer: It sends a message to the background script, which can use any API its permissions allow.

title: How Google crawls, renders and indexes a JavaScript page
purpose: Show that Google indexes the rendered HTML, so a tool must show you the page after JavaScript ran.
explanation: Googlebot checks robots.txt, fetches the raw HTML and queues pages with status 200 for rendering. A headless Chromium then runs the JavaScript. Google indexes the rendered HTML. A page blocked in robots.txt is never rendered, so an SEO extension that reads only the source HTML misses what Google sees.
alt: Flowchart: a URL in the crawl queue is checked against robots.txt. If blocked it is skipped. If allowed, raw HTML is fetched, pages with status 200 are queued for rendering, a headless Chromium runs the JavaScript, and the rendered HTML is indexed.

learning_check.question: Which HTML does Google index, and what happens to a URL that robots.txt disallows?
learning_check.answer: Google indexes the rendered HTML. A disallowed URL is skipped and its JavaScript is not rendered.

title: axe-core module map
purpose: Show the six analyzed parts of axe-core and which part calls which.
explanation: The engine run is the centre. It starts a frame job for iframes and runs every rule on this page. Rules call small checks, such as heading order and colour contrast. Tests guard the engine, and the build ships one bundle that CI tests. Accessibility extensions wrap this engine.
alt: Flowchart: engine-run points to frame-messaging for iframe jobs, to the headings and landmarks rules for any, all and none checks, and to the color-contrast check. A tests node points to engine-run with a dotted line, and the build node points to engine-run as the shipped bundle.

learning_check.question: Which part of axe-core handles iframes, and which part decides if text contrast is enough?
learning_check.answer: Frame messaging handles iframes. The colour-contrast check, called by the engine run, decides contrast.

title: One axe.run call from start to report
purpose: Show how one scan moves through the engine and where a check can answer 'cannot tell'.
explanation: The caller starts a scan. The engine sets a running flag, builds the page context, and queues two jobs: scan child frames and run the rules here. Each rule runs checks per element. A check returns true, false or undefined. The engine merges results, runs the after step, builds the report, and resets the flag.
alt: Sequence diagram: the caller calls axe.run, run.js sets the running flag and calls runRules, which queues a frame job and a rule job. Rules run any, all and none checks that return true, false or undefined. Results are merged, finalized, reported to the caller and the engine is reset.

learning_check.question: What are the three possible answers of a check, and which one means a person must look?
learning_check.answer: True, false and undefined. Undefined is reported as incomplete and needs human review.

title: What React DevTools and Redux DevTools read
purpose: Show in one static picture where each framework devtools extension gets its data, for readers without JavaScript.
explanation: On a website built with React, React DevTools adds the Components and Profiler panels; in Components you select a component and edit its props or state. In Redux, a dispatched action passes the middleware in array order, the reducer returns the next state, and the store sends the action and state to the Redux DevTools extension while the devTools option is true, its default. With false, the store still updates but the extension receives nothing (react.dev React Developer Tools; redux.js.org Configuring Your Store).
alt: Flowchart in two parts. React DevTools: the Components panel selects a component, its props or state are edited, and the page shows the new value; the Profiler panel finds performance problems. Redux: dispatch todoAdded goes to the thunk middleware, then the logger added with concat, then the reducer returns the next state; a devTools option decision sends action and state to the Redux DevTools extension when true or an options object, and sends nothing when false while the store still updates.

learning_check.question: Which configureStore setting stops the Redux DevTools extension from receiving actions?
learning_check.answer: devTools: false. The store still updates, but the integration with the extension is off.

title: Framework devtools show components and store actions
purpose: See what the React DevTools panels let you change and how a dispatched Redux action reaches the store and the Redux DevTools extension.
explanation: Framework devtools read what the framework keeps behind the DOM: React components with their props and state, and each Redux action with the state after it. Redux sends that data to the extension only while the devTools option is on.
alt: React DevTools adds the Components and Profiler panels on websites built with React; in Components you select a component and edit its props or state. In a Redux todo app, configureStore connects the store to the Redux DevTools extension by default. A dispatched todoAdded action passes the thunk middleware, then a logger added with concat, then the reducer returns the next state, and the store sends the action and state to the extension. With devTools set to false the store still updates, but the extension receives nothing. Safari uses the standalone react-devtools package.

learning_check.question: You set devTools to false in configureStore and dispatch todoAdded. What changes in the app, and what does the Redux DevTools extension show?
learning_check.answer: The reducer still returns the next state with the new todo, but the extension receives no actions and no state, because the integration is off.

learning_check.question: The React DevTools extension is installed. You open a plain HTML page that does not use React. Which panels do you get?
learning_check.answer: Only the built-in DevTools panels. React DevTools adds the Components and Profiler panels when you visit a website built with React. A page without React has no components for it to read.

title: Pass, fail or incomplete for contrast and heading checks
purpose: Show how an automated contrast or heading check reaches pass, fail or incomplete, and what stays for a person.
explanation: If the tool cannot see the real colors or the previous heading, it reports incomplete. Otherwise it measures: the contrast ratio, rounded down, against 4.5:1 or 3:1, and the heading level against the previous one. A pass covers only that rule; a person still judges meaning and real use.
alt: Flowchart: an element first goes to incomplete when colors or the previous heading are unknown. Otherwise the tool compares the contrast ratio with 4.5:1 or 3:1 and the heading level with the previous level, giving pass or fail. Even a pass leaves text on images, heading meaning and keyboard use for a person.

learning_check.question: Gray #777777 text on white measures 4.48:1. Normal size. Which outcome does the check give?
learning_check.answer: Fail. The ratio is rounded down to 4.47, which is below 4.5:1, and there is no rounding up.

title: Pass, fail or incomplete: contrast and heading checks
purpose: See how an automated accessibility check decides pass, fail or incomplete for color contrast and heading order, and what it leaves for a person.
explanation: A rule decides only what it can measure. When it cannot see the real colors or the previous heading, it answers incomplete instead of guessing, and a person reviews it.
alt: An accessibility scan gives three answers: pass, fail or incomplete. The contrast ratio is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05). Normal text needs at least 4.5:1, large text at least 3:1. Gray #767676 on white scores 4.54 and passes; #777777 scores 4.47 and fails, because axe rounds down. A background image, an overlapping element, one-character text or an empty input gives incomplete. Heading order fails when a heading is more than one level deeper than the one before it. A person still judges text on images, heading meaning, and keyboard and screen reader use.

learning_check.question: Gray #777777 normal-size text on white measures 4.48:1. What does the contrast check report, and why?
learning_check.answer: Fail. The ratio is rounded down to 4.47, which is below the 4.5:1 that normal text needs.

title: Change colors and headings, predict the accessibility check
purpose: Predict whether an automated contrast or heading-order check passes, fails or returns incomplete, and name what a person must still review.
explanation: Step through an animated walkthrough, change the simulation and answer the checkpoints. Predict whether an automated contrast or heading-order check passes, fails or returns incomplete, and name what a person must still review.
alt: A guided walkthrough of how an axe-style scan judges color contrast and heading order, paused for predictions, with a stepper where the learner changes text colors, text size and heading levels. Gray #767676 on white passes at 4.54:1; #777777 fails at 4.47:1 because the ratio is rounded down; large text needs only 3:1; text on a background image or a heading whose previous heading cannot be found returns incomplete. No rule judges heading meaning, so a person still reviews.

learning_check.question: Normal-size gray #777777 text on white measures 4.478:1. What does the color-contrast check report?
learning_check.answer: Fail: 4.47 is below 4.5. The threshold is a hard minimum. axe rounds the ratio down to 4.47 before it reports it, so a near miss never shows as a pass. Incomplete is only for cases where the colors cannot be known.

title: Where the crawler and each SEO tool read the page
purpose: Show that the source HTML and the rendered DOM are different stages, and that each tool reads only one of them.
explanation: Google first reads the server response: the status code and the source HTML. Headless Chromium then runs the JavaScript, and Google indexes the rendered DOM. View source shows the source HTML. An SEO extension reads the rendered DOM, so it sees titles and JSON-LD that scripts added, but not the raw status code. Check both stages.
alt: Flowchart from left to right: the server response with its status code leads to the source HTML, then headless Chromium runs JavaScript, then the rendered DOM with title and JSON-LD goes to the Google index. View source reads the source HTML. An SEO extension reads the rendered DOM.

learning_check.question: Your page title is set only by JavaScript. View source shows no title. Which tool shows what Google indexes?
learning_check.answer: The SEO extension, because it reads the rendered DOM, and Google indexes the rendered HTML after the JavaScript runs.

title: A vetted team extension profile
purpose: Show how a team profile groups vetted extensions and which manifest permission each group asks for.
explanation: When a built-in DevTools panel does the job, the team uses the panel and installs no extension. Otherwise the extension passes a manifest review before it joins the team profile. The profile has four groups: framework panels, audit checkers such as axe-core and Retire.js, design helpers, and request rules. Design helpers need host access or activeTab. Request rules need the declarativeNetRequest permission.
alt: Flowchart: a need for a tool splits two ways. If a built-in panel does the job, it leads to the built-in panels. If an extension adds data, it leads to a manifest review, then to the team profile, which branches into four groups: framework panels, audit checkers, design helpers and request rules. Dotted lines send design helpers back to the review for host access or activeTab, and request rules back for the declarativeNetRequest permission.

learning_check.question: A CSS helper wants to change styles on every site you open. Which permission do you check before it joins the profile?
learning_check.answer: Its host access: a content script can read and change the DOM of every page its manifest matches. Narrow host access, or activeTab for injection on demand, fits the job better.

title: Pick the right tool for each security symptom
purpose: Choose the right check for three security symptoms of a page (an old library, a missing CSP header, an extension that asks for every site) and put the checks in one quick order.
explanation: Each symptom needs the tool that can see it: a version needs a vulnerability database, a policy needs the response header, and access needs the extension manifest.
alt: A quick security pass on a page has three checks. Retire.js finds libraries with known vulnerabilities. The Content-Security-Policy response header shows which scripts the page allows. The match patterns and permissions of an extension show which pages its content scripts can read. Each deep dive shows the result of a weak choice and of the right choice.

learning_check.question: A page loads an old copy of a JavaScript library. Which check tells you whether that version has known vulnerabilities?
learning_check.answer: Retire.js: it compares the library version with its list of versions that have known vulnerabilities.

slides.notes: State the task: three symptoms, three tools, and one short order for a security pass.
Each symptom is a different kind of fact: a version, a response header, and a permission in a manifest.
Open one deep dive per symptom. Each shows a weak choice, its result, and the right check. Back returns here.
Start with what the page loads, then what the page allows, then what your own tools can read.
A wrong tool gives a calm answer to the wrong question. Ask what kind of fact the symptom is, then pick the tool that reads it.
The Elements panel shows the script tag and maybe a version, but not which versions have known vulnerabilities.
Retire.js detects JavaScript libraries and reports versions with known vulnerabilities. It runs as a command line tool and inside Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP.
The server sends the policy in the Content-Security-Policy response header. A meta element can also set a policy, but it lacks some features.
MDN recommends a strict policy with nonces or hashes for scripts, because an allowlist of hosts is hard to keep safe.
The manifest match patterns choose the pages. A content script runs in each matching page and reads its DOM.
Access to all sites lets the content script read every page you open. activeTab gives access only after you invoke the extension.

title: Choose the check for each security symptom
purpose: Pick the tool that can see each security symptom of a page and order a quick security pass.
explanation: Choose a path through the deck and open the deep dives. Pick the tool that can see each security symptom of a page and order a quick security pass.
alt: A branching deck shows three security symptoms of one page: an old library version, a missing Content-Security-Policy header, and a helper extension that asks for access to all sites. Each deep dive shows what a weak check misses and what the right check shows: Retire.js, the response headers, or the extension manifest. The deck ends with one order for a quick pass.

learning_check.question: The page loads jQuery from an old file. Which check tells you whether that version has known vulnerabilities?
learning_check.answer: Scan the page with Retire.js. Retire.js detects the library and its version and compares it with a list of versions that have known vulnerabilities. The Elements panel shows the tag but has no vulnerability data.

title: Extension permission audit flow
purpose: Show how manifest files and a JSON policy become a verdict per extension.
explanation: main.ts reads each manifest.json and policy.json. auditManifest runs three rule functions for broad hosts, risky APIs and content scripts on all sites, adds their points, and verdictFor maps the score to approve, review or reject. formatReport prints the table and the exit code lets CI block a rejection.
alt: Flowchart: manifest.json files go to main.ts, then auditManifest, then the three rule functions, then verdictFor, then formatReport.

learning_check.question: Where do the point values and thresholds come from, and why?
learning_check.answer: From policy.json, so a team can change what counts as risky without editing code.

title: Release a11y and SEO check flow
purpose: Show how saved pages become findings with three outcomes and a CI exit code.
explanation: main.ts loops over the pages in pages.json. readHead and checkSeo judge the head tags, and runAxe runs axe-core in jsdom while toFindings keeps violation, pass and incomplete. newViolations compares the violations with baseline.json, and main.ts exits 1 only when a violation is new.
alt: Flowchart: pages.json and saved HTML go to main.ts, which feeds readHead with checkSeo and runAxe with toFindings into one findings list, then newViolations against baseline.json, then exit 0 or 1.

learning_check.question: Why does a color-contrast result in this project not fail the build?
learning_check.answer: jsdom has no layout, so axe returns it as incomplete (needs review), and only new violations change the exit code.

title: toolkit-profile CLI layers
purpose: Show which layer depends on which in the toolkit-profile CLI.
explanation: The interface layer (Cli, TextRenderer) calls the application layer: use cases, checks, ProfileLoader and ManifestScorer. Application code uses only the domain: Policy, Profile, Outcome, Summary and the ports. The infrastructure layer implements the ports with files, jsdom and axe-core. Arrows point inward, so the rules never import a disk or a DOM library.
alt: Flowchart: main.ts wires the interface layer and the infrastructure layer. The interface layer depends on the application layer. The application layer and the infrastructure layer both depend on the domain layer, which depends on nothing. Dependencies point inward.

learning_check.question: Which layer would you change to read pages from a live URL instead of a file, and which layers stay the same?
learning_check.answer: Add an adapter in the infrastructure layer for the page source port. The domain, application and interface layers stay the same.

title: One run of the toolkit-profile CLI
purpose: Show the order of a run and where it stops early.
explanation: Cli asks ProfileLoader to load the policy and profile. A bad file ends the run with exit code 2. Otherwise ValidateProfileUseCase judges each extension. One failing extension ends the run with exit code 1 before any page check. If none fails, AuditPageUseCase runs each Check on one shared context and returns pass, fail or review rows.
alt: Sequence diagram: Cli calls ProfileLoader. A policy or profile error ends the run with exit 2. Otherwise ValidateProfileUseCase runs. If an extension fails, the run stops with exit 1. If none fails, AuditPageUseCase runs each Check and returns rows to Cli.

learning_check.question: A profile lists one extension with debugger and all-sites access. Do the page checks run?
learning_check.answer: No. The extension scores above the reject limit, so Cli prints Profile rejected and exits with code 1 before AuditPageUseCase starts.

title: toolkit-profile CLI deployment
purpose: Show what the process reads and writes.
explanation: The tool is one Node.js process, or one Docker image with the same entry point. It reads saved files and three environment variables. It writes the report to stdout, JSON logs to stderr and an exit code of 0, 1 or 2. There is no server, no database and no network call.
alt: Flowchart: saved profile, manifests, page and headers files, plus the environment variables TOOLKIT_POLICY, TOOLKIT_LOG_LEVEL and TOOLKIT_STRICT, feed one Node process. The process writes the report to stdout, JSON logs to stderr and an exit code.

learning_check.question: Where do the report and the logs go, and why does it matter in CI?
learning_check.answer: The report goes to stdout and logs to stderr, so CI can save the report without log lines mixed in. The exit code tells CI whether to fail the build.
